items.name: Text formats such as JSON versus binary formats
items.explanation: JSON writes data as readable text, so it is easy to debug but verbose to send and slower to encode and decode. A binary format such as protocol buffers writes compact bytes that people cannot read directly, and both sides need to agree on the schema.

assumedBy.quote: While JSON has served us well in terms of broad programming language support and human-readability (which eases debuggability), its runtime performance has been far from ideal.

items.name: Field numbers in a protocol buffers schema
items.explanation: A protocol buffers message gives each field a number, and that number, not the field name, identifies the field in the bytes on the wire. It cannot change once the message is in use.

assumedBy.quote: Protobuf serialization relies on both strongly-typed data as well as explicit field numbers

sources.title: Protocol Buffers Language Guide (proto 3): Assigning Field Numbers

items.name: HTTP headers such as Content-Type and Accept
items.explanation: A header is a named line sent with a request or response. Content-Type says what format the body is in, and Accept says which response formats the client prefers. A custom header, like a version, works the same way.

assumedBy.quote: These configurations enabled the client to encode the payload using Protobuf instead of JSON and set the content-type header to Protobuf, or set the accept header to instruct the server to prefer Protobuf over JSON for encoding responses.
Users can override the version of any single request by manually setting the Stripe-Version header, or upgrade their account’s pinned version from Stripe’s dashboard.

sources.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics (6.3 Header Fields, 8.3 Content-Type, 12.5.1 Accept)

items.name: Latency percentiles such as P99
items.explanation: A percentile is the latency that a given share of requests finish within. P99 describes the slowest 1% of requests, which an average hides.

assumedBy.quote: Below is the P99 latency comparison chart from benchmarking Protobuf against JSON when servers are under heavy load.

sources.title: Monitoring Distributed Systems (Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 6)

items.name: A GraphQL query as a selection of fields on typed objects
items.explanation: A GraphQL query starts at a root type and lists the fields wanted, down to leaf values. Because every field belongs to a type in the schema, a server can read a query and know what it asks for before running it.

assumedBy.quote: By identifying each type used in a query, we can calculate its cost.

items.name: GraphQL connections, edges and cursors
items.explanation: A connection is how GraphQL exposes a list that is read in pages. It holds edges, each with a node and a cursor, plus page information such as whether a next page exists. The cursor marks a position in the list.

assumedBy.quote: Connections express one-to-many relationships in GraphQL.
